arguments.question: What if I raise my cappuccino from €3.50 to €3.80 next month?

content.text:
Decision template: Price change on one item (price_change). Compares a new price with the current one: what each sale leaves after VAT and ingredients, how many sales you could lose before you are worse off, and what different customer reactions would mean per week and per month.

Numbers to ask for, one at a time (6 needed):
1. Which item are you thinking of repricing? [item] (why: One item at a time keeps the effect easy to see and to measure.)
2. What does it cost today? [current_price] (why: The starting point for the comparison.)
3. What new price are you considering? [new_price] (why: The change you want to rehearse.)
4. Roughly how many do you sell in a week? Your till's item report shows it. [units_per_week] (why: The effect of a few cents depends on how many you sell.)
5. What do the ingredients and cup cost per item? For a flat white: coffee, milk, cup and lid. [unit_cost] (why: A price rise goes straight to what each sale earns, so this tells you how much margin you gain.)
6. What do you think would really happen to sales? Small rises often lose a few percent. [volume_likely] (why: This is the guess the test will check.)
Optional (a labelled guess is used if the owner does not know): Your Kiez (neighbourhood in Berlin) [kiez]; VAT on this item [vat_rate]; Change in sales: cautious guess [volume_low]; Change in sales: optimistic guess [volume_high]; Length of the test (days) [test_days]; Staff hours a week paid at or near the minimum wage [minimum_wage_hours_per_week].
Kiez (optional, shapes the imagined customers): Neukölln, Kreuzberg, Friedrichshain, Prenzlauer Berg, Mitte, Wedding, Moabit, Schöneberg, Charlottenburg, Friedenau, Pankow, Lichtenberg, Treptow, Tempelhof, Steglitz, Köpenick, Spandau, Weißensee, or other.

Start by asking: "Which item are you thinking of repricing?"
Or show how it works first with the demo café (Café Lindenblatt (demo café, Berlin-Neukölln), made-up numbers labelled as demo data): call whatif_run_scenarios with demo: true.
Berlin events the owner can add to a rehearsal later (imagined, not facts): BVG strike: no U-Bahn, trams or buses for a day, so many people work from home.; It rains all week.; Heatwave: 32 °C all week.; Roadworks (a Baustelle) outside: the pavement is half closed for a week.; Berlin school holidays start: many families and students are away.; A new café opens two doors down with an €8.50 lunch.; A big Kiez street festival from Friday to Sunday: the street is full of people.; The Christmas market opens on the square round the corner..

ask_first.label: Item
ask_first.ask: Which item are you thinking of repricing?
ask_first.why: One item at a time keeps the effect easy to see and to measure.

ask_first.label: Current price (what customers pay)
ask_first.why: The starting point for the comparison.

ask_first.label: New price (what customers would pay)
ask_first.ask: What new price are you considering?
ask_first.why: The change you want to rehearse.

ask_first.label: Sales per week now
ask_first.ask: Roughly how many do you sell in a week? Your till's item report shows it.
ask_first.why: The effect of a few cents depends on how many you sell.

ask_first.label: Ingredients and packaging per item
ask_first.ask: What do the ingredients and cup cost per item? For a flat white: coffee, milk, cup and lid.
ask_first.why: A price rise goes straight to what each sale earns, so this tells you how much margin you gain.

ask_first.label: Change in sales: your likely guess
ask_first.ask: What do you think would really happen to sales? Small rises often lose a few percent.
ask_first.why: This is the guess the test will check.

optional_fields.label: Your Kiez (neighbourhood in Berlin)
optional_fields.ask: Which Kiez is your café in?
optional_fields.why: The imagined customers in the rehearsal come from your Kiez. It does not change the money sums.

optional_fields.label: VAT on this item
optional_fields.ask: Which VAT rate is on this item? Food is 7%. Drinks are 19%, milk drinks drunk in the café included. Only milk drinks sold to take away with at least 75% milk are 7%. If you are a Kleinunternehmer and charge no VAT, enter 0.
optional_fields.why: VAT is not yours to keep. What-IF works with prices after VAT, so the margins show what really stays with you.

optional_fields.label: Change in sales: cautious guess
optional_fields.ask: If customers really disliked it, how much would sales drop? For example −10%.
optional_fields.why: Price changes lose some sales. A range keeps the guess honest.

optional_fields.label: Change in sales: optimistic guess
optional_fields.ask: And if nobody minded at all?

optional_fields.label: Length of the test (days)
optional_fields.ask: How many days would you try the new price before deciding? Two weeks is usual.
optional_fields.why: Long enough for regulars to react, short enough to change back.

optional_fields.label: Staff hours a week paid at or near the minimum wage
optional_fields.ask: How many staff hours a week do you pay at or near the minimum wage (€13.90 an hour)? Your rota or payroll shows it. Leave it out if this price change has nothing to do with wages.
optional_fields.why: From 1 January 2027 the minimum wage rises to €14.60, so each of these hours costs €0.70 more. What-IF sets that against what the new price brings, so you see whether the price covers the rise.

coaching: Reflect the question back in one sentence and say What-IF will compare a cautious, an expected and an optimistic outcome; it does not predict the future.
Ask for the numbers ONE at a time, in the order given, saying why each matters. Accept rough answers; 'I don't know' is fine for optional ones (a labelled guess is used).
After each answer call whatif_check_inputs; it returns the next question. When ready, call whatif_run_scenarios and share the report link.

Explain break-even and the worst case in plain words, then offer: rehearse with imagined customers (whatif_rehearsal_start), try another number (whatif_what_changed), or plan a small test (whatif_plan_test). Pass them the `state` from the last result.
Every figure has a source tag, the same as on the report: "Your number", "A guess", "Calculated", "Imagined" or "Demo data". Keep them apart when you talk.

arguments.question: What if I raise my cappuccino from €3.50 to €3.80 next month?

content.text:
Café Morgenrot, Kreuzberg: What if I raise my cappuccino from €3.50 to €3.80 next month?
Break-even (the one number to remember): At €3.80 each cappuccino leaves €2.34 after VAT and ingredients instead of €2.09, so you can sell up to 48 fewer a week (10.7% of 450) and still make as much as now. Lose more than that and you are worse off.
Three possible outcomes (calculated from the owner's numbers and guesses):
- Cautious: If sales change by −12% (about 396 a week), you make €14 less a week than now: €28 less over the 14-day test and about €60 a month.
- Expected: If sales change by −5% (about 428 a week), you make €60 more a week than now: €120 over the 14-day test and about €259 a month.
- Optimistic: If sales change by 0% (about 450 a week), you make €113 more a week than now: €225 over the 14-day test and about €487 a month.
Worst case: If sales fell by 12% (your cautious guess), the 14-day test would leave you €28 worse off than keeping the old price. You can change the price back at any time, so that is what is at stake.
Biggest uncertainty: Whether sales change by −12% or 0% changes the test result by €253, more than anything else. That is what your test should measure: count the cappuccino sales each week.
Watch out:
- At your cautious guess (−12%) the new price earns less than today (break-even is −10.7%). That is the risk the test checks.
Public facts the maths uses: VAT on drinks, milk drinks drunk in the café included 19% (§ 12 Abs. 1 und Abs. 2 Nr. 15 UStG, 2026-01-01); VAT on milk drinks sold to take away with at least 75% milk (not plant drinks such as oat); an older rule, unchanged in 2026 7% (§ 12 Abs. 2 Nr. 1 UStG mit Anlage 2 Nr. 35, 2026-01-01); VAT on food in cafés and restaurants (eat-in and take-away) 7% since 1 January 2026 (Steueränderungsgesetz 2025, § 12 Abs. 2 Nr. 15 UStG, 2026-01-01).
Next step: let the owner move one guess (whatif_what_changed), rehearse it with imagined customers (whatif_rehearsal_start), or plan a small test (whatif_plan_test).
Next calls (whatif_what_changed, whatif_rehearsal_start, whatif_plan_test, whatif_log_result) can take `state` = this result's state or the report link instead of template and inputs.

lessons: A rise of 30 cents looks small, but ingredients cost the same: after 19% VAT, €0.25 of it is extra margin on every sale. Each cappuccino leaves €2.34 instead of €2.09, 12.0% more per sale.
Break-even is the number to beat: you can lose up to 48 sales a week (10.7%) before you are worse off. Your likely guess is −5% (about 23 fewer), inside that. The test checks the guess.
At your cautious guess (−12%) the 14-day test costs about €28. A price can be changed back the next morning, which makes this one of the cheapest things to test.
The number that matters most: whether sales change by −12% or 0% changes the test result by €253, more than anything else. That is what your test should measure: count the cappuccino sales each week.
This method works for any decision: write down your numbers, work out the break-even, then run a small test with a limit to check the one guess that matters most.
nextQuestions: Which VAT rate is on your cappuccino? What-IF used 19%, the rate for drinks, milk drinks drunk in the café included. Food is 7%. Milk drinks with at least 75% milk sold to take away are 7% too, but only that take-away share. Your Steuerberater can confirm.
Look at the last 4 weeks in your till's item report: is 450 a week steady, or does it swing? A steady baseline makes the test easier to read.
What would regulars buy instead? If a cheaper drink's sales rise during the test, people are trading down rather than leaving.
warnings: At your cautious guess (−12%) the new price earns less than today (break-even is −10.7%). That is the risk the test checks.

perStep.plain: Each percentage point of sales is about 4.5 sales a week, which moves the test result by about €21 and the monthly result by about €46.

lessons: A rise of 30 cents looks small, but ingredients cost the same: after 19% VAT, €0.25 of it is extra margin on every sale. Each cappuccino leaves €2.34 instead of €2.09, 12.0% more per sale.
Break-even is the number to beat: you can lose up to 48 sales a week (10.7%) before you are worse off. Your likely guess is −8% (about 36 fewer), inside that. The test checks the guess.
At your cautious guess (−12%) the 14-day test costs about €28. A price can be changed back the next morning, which makes this one of the cheapest things to test.
The number that matters most: whether sales change by −12% or 0% changes the test result by €253, more than anything else. That is what your test should measure: count the cappuccino sales each week.
This method works for any decision: write down your numbers, work out the break-even, then run a small test with a limit to check the one guess that matters most.
nextQuestions: Which VAT rate is on your cappuccino? What-IF used 19%, the rate for drinks, milk drinks drunk in the café included. Food is 7%. Milk drinks with at least 75% milk sold to take away are 7% too, but only that take-away share. Your Steuerberater can confirm.
Look at the last 4 weeks in your till's item report: is 450 a week steady, or does it swing? A steady baseline makes the test easier to read.
What would regulars buy instead? If a cheaper drink's sales rise during the test, people are trading down rather than leaving.
warnings: At your cautious guess (−12%) the new price earns less than today (break-even is −10.7%). That is the risk the test checks.

reactions.thought: I saw €3.80 when I tapped my card. Fine. This is the place that let me wait out the rain for two hours, I'm not leaving over thirty cents. When I buy one for a colleague too, I'll feel it a bit.
reactions.diary: Cappuccino is €3.80 now. Paid it without much thought; still my after-meeting spot.

reactions.thought: Money's tight and I'm here three afternoons a week, so thirty cents a cup adds up. Nobody said a word, which is about what I expect after the soup and the shrug. I told the Späti owner on my way out.
reactions.saysPublicly: Morgenrot put the cappuccino up to €3.80. Thirty cents more for the same cup, and not a word about it.
reactions.questionForOwner: Can I still sit at the socket table for an afternoon with one cappuccino, or do you expect more now?
reactions.diary: Morgenrot raised the cappuccino to €3.80 without saying anything. Told the Späti owner.

reactions.thought: I asked Jule at the counter and she just shrugged: costs went up. Fine, it's still my place, I'll pay €3.80. But I bring the cup back every day, so I did wonder if that counts for anything.
reactions.questionForOwner: I bring my cup back every day. Is there anything off for that?
reactions.diary: Cappuccino €3.80 from Monday. Asked at the counter; costs went up, they said.

reactions.thought: I was away a few days and came back to €3.80 on the board. Thirty cents doesn't decide it for me; my paper and my cappuccino here do. The new place does lunches. I'm not queueing there to find out.

reactions.diary: Came back to €3.80. Had my cappuccino as usual, cushion and all.

quotes.name: Aiko
quotes.text: Morgenrot put the cappuccino up to €3.80. Thirty cents more for the same cup, and not a word about it.

quotes.name: Barbara
quotes.text: A queue of four on Thursday, so I read the front page while I waited. €3.80 is just the price now. I left the review cards alone; all they'd get from me is a note about the chairs.

quotes.name: Omar
quotes.text: Come to Morgenrot after the meeting: best cappuccino round here, worth the €3.80. Just don't go at nine, the queue is long.

quotes.name: Omar
quotes.text: A queue of four at nine is exactly what I avoid, so I came back after the meeting with the new colleague from HR. I told him it's worth it. Thirty cents never decided anything for me.

quotes.name: Samir
quotes.text: Staff who know your name and a great cappuccino to go. A bit dearer since the rise to €3.80, but still my morning stop.

quotes.name: Samir
quotes.text: The staff put out review cards, so I filled one in for them while I waited in the queue. They deserve a good one. I mentioned the price, though, because it's the first thing people see now.

questionsForOwner: Can I still sit at the socket table for an afternoon with one cappuccino, or do you expect more now?
I bring my cup back every day. Is there anything off for that?
If it costs more now, could the chairs get a bit softer? I still bring my own cushion.
Are you going to do anything for lunch now that the new place is two doors down?
Would you do a cheaper second cup for people who stay all afternoon?
Do you notice when a regular stops coming as often?
checkWithRealCustomers: Watch the first ten cappuccino customers after the change: do they look at the board, say something, or order something else?
Ask three regulars directly whether €3.80 for a cappuccino changes how often they come. 0 of 3 imagined regulars bought less.
Ask staff to jot down any comments about the price in the first week: 2 imagined customers said something out loud or online.
Check what the two nearest cafés charge for a cappuccino: 1 imagined customer went elsewhere.

Have a friendly answer ready for questions like "Can I still sit at the socket table for an afternoon with one cappuccino, or do you expect more now?" and "I bring my cup back every day. Is there anything off for that?".
summary.caveat: These imagined customers were played by an AI in your chat, one at a time, from short briefs; they are not data. They show reactions worth checking, not what will happen. Nothing here is counted in the money maths. The mix of people is a rough guess for Kreuzberg, not statistics.

content.text:
Test plan: 14-day price test: cappuccino at €3.80.
Charge €3.80 for 14 days and count cappuccino sales each week against your baseline of 450. Your guess is −8%; keep it if you still sell at least 402 a week (a drop of up to 10.7%). Keep everything else the same.
Before you start:
- Take one normal week from your till's item report as your baseline (about 450 a week), and look at the weeks before it to see whether it swings.
- Change the price on the menu board, the till and any online menu (Google Maps, delivery apps) on the same day.
- Note the weekly sales of the nearest cheaper alternative too (for example filter coffee), so you can see whether people trade down.
Measure:
- Sales of cappuccino per week: The till's item report, same weekday to same weekday, so the comparison is fair.
- Sales of the nearest alternative: The till's item report: if they rise while yours fall, customers are trading down rather than leaving.
- Comments about the price: A tally sheet by the till: one stroke per comment, with a word or two about what was said.
Check-ins:
- Day 3: Is the new price on the till, the board and online? Note any comments so far.
- Day 7: Compare the first week with your baseline: you can lose up to 48 a week (10.7%) before you are worse off.
- Day 14: Compare the weekly average with your baseline, apply the decision rule below and log the result in What-IF.
Decision rule:
- Keep: Sales fall by 10.7% or less (you still sell at least 402 a week): keep the new price.
- Tweak: They fall by more than 10.7% but not more than 16.0% (from 378 to under 402 a week): try a smaller rise, about €3.65, for another 14 days.
- Stop: They fall by more than 16.0% (fewer than 378 a week): go back to €3.50.
Cost cap: Switch back early if sales fall below 378 a week in the first full week. At your cautious guess (−12%) the whole test costs about €28.
After the test, call whatif_log_result with what was measured and this result's `state`.

plan.title: 14-day price test: cappuccino at €3.80
before: Take one normal week from your till's item report as your baseline (about 450 a week), and look at the weeks before it to see whether it swings.
Change the price on the menu board, the till and any online menu (Google Maps, delivery apps) on the same day.
Note the weekly sales of the nearest cheaper alternative too (for example filter coffee), so you can see whether people trade down.
during: Keep everything else the same: same recipe, same size, no special offers on cappuccino.
Run it for the full 14 days, so regulars have time to react.
If a regular asks about the new price, explain it honestly and briefly.

measure.how: The till's item report, same weekday to same weekday, so the comparison is fair.
The till's item report: if they rise while yours fall, customers are trading down rather than leaving.
A tally sheet by the till: one stroke per comment, with a word or two about what was said.

checkIns.look: Is the new price on the till, the board and online? Note any comments so far.
Compare the first week with your baseline: you can lose up to 48 a week (10.7%) before you are worse off.
Compare the weekly average with your baseline, apply the decision rule below and log the result in What-IF.

decisionRule.keep: Sales fall by 10.7% or less (you still sell at least 402 a week): keep the new price.
decisionRule.tweak: They fall by more than 10.7% but not more than 16.0% (from 378 to under 402 a week): try a smaller rise, about €3.65, for another 14 days.
decisionRule.stop: They fall by more than 16.0% (fewer than 378 a week): go back to €3.50.

plan.costCap: Switch back early if sales fall below 378 a week in the first full week. At your cautious guess (−12%) the whole test costs about €28.
plan.plain: Charge €3.80 for 14 days and count cappuccino sales each week against your baseline of 450. Your guess is −8%; keep it if you still sell at least 402 a week (a drop of up to 10.7%). Keep everything else the same.
